Bump please.  Is there a workaround, or fix for this?

**Root cause**: Ubuntu's default `~/.bashrc` has a guard at the top that exits immediately for non-interactive shells:

```bash
# If not running interactively, don't do anything
case $- in
    *i*) ;;
      *) return;;
esac
```

OpenCode spawns bash as a **non-interactive**, **non-login** shell for its bash tool, so `~/.bashrc` returns early and never loads nvm.

**Fix**: Move nvm initialization above the interactive guard in `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
# nvm - load before interactive check
export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"
[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"

# Ubuntu's default interactive guard
case $- in
    *i*) ;;
      *) return;;
esac

# ... rest of .bashrc (prompt, aliases, etc.)
```

**Why this works**: nvm loads for both interactive and non-interactive shells, while prompt/alias configurations remain interactive-only.


run `source ~/.bashrc && your command` everytime

It’s very likely that your PATH places **Windows PowerShell (powershell.exe)** ahead of your **modern PowerShell (pwsh.exe)** installation. I’ve seen this exact issue on other systems, and the combination of PATH order plus installation type is usually the culprit.

Winget no longer installs a real standalone package — it redirects you to the **Store/MSIX** version of PowerShell. That build is sandboxed and relies on shims. Removing it and installing the **MSI distribution** (explicitly the ~200 MB MSI — *not* MSIX, *not* MSIXBundle) consistently fixes the problem.

The Store/MSIX version installs shims that *can* launch modern PowerShell, but they do **not** cover the canonical path: %ProgramFiles%\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe

A lot of applications are hardcoded to look exactly there. Notice the executable is **pwsh.exe**, not `powershell.exe`. The shims shadow `powershell.exe` and the `powershell` alias, but the correct modern binary is always `pwsh`. Depending on whether you installed via Store or MSI, the alias/executable mapping flips — which is why this feels chaotic.

Also, don’t worry about updates: the **official MSI installation is serviced automatically**. On Windows, Windows Update handles it; on other platforms, the runtime’s own updater takes care of it.

Quick recap of the ask: this adds an **optional** `Gate` service in `PermissionV2`'s `evaluateInput`, consulted right after the effect resolves, so a plugin can turn a *would-auto-approve* into an interactive `ask`. It's a no-op with no hard dependency when no provider is registered, so it's inert unless something opts in. The PR is honestly scoped to just the core hook point — wiring the `permission.ask` plugin hook through it touches core's location-service layering, which I left as a maintainer call.

Context for why it's useful: it's the one interception `tool.execute.before` can't do (block-only, no human prompt). I'm using it to drive a vendor-neutral guardrail layer ([OpenGuardrails](https://openguardrails.com)) — same enforcement point I'm wiring into Kilo CLI ([Kilo-Org/kilocode#11619](https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/pull/11619)).

Dropping this here in case anyone's still stuck. I hit this constantly after auto-compaction and got tired of starting a fresh session every time, so I wrote a small OpenCode plugin to work around it:

https://github.com/viiqswim/opencode-compaction-guard

Add one line to your opencode.json:

```jsonc
"plugin": ["opencode-compaction-guard@latest"]
```

(or just drop the single .mjs into ~/.config/opencode/plugin/, the README has both ways).

Roughly how it works:

- Before each request, and before compaction, it finds any tool call stuck in pending/running and turns it into an error result, so every tool_use still has a matching tool_result.
- If the 400 fires anyway, it catches the session error and reverts the failed turn for you (debounced so it can't loop, and you can /unrevert if you want it back). The session keeps going instead of dying.

One thing I want to be upfront about, since it lines up with the root cause in this thread: that first part only covers the interrupted-tool case. The post-compaction slice you all described happens further down the pipeline than a plugin hook can reach, so for that one it leans on the auto-revert instead of actually preventing it. So it's a band-aid, not a real fix. The proper fix still has to happen in opencode itself.

The two pieces are borrowed from #8497 (pending/running to error result) and #1662 (revert on error), just packaged up so it's easy to install.

Really good writeup. The normalizeMessages split is exactly the kind of thing a plugin can't catch, since it happens after the hooks have already run.

While the transform.ts fix is pending, I put together a plugin that at least stops sessions from getting permanently wedged:

https://github.com/viiqswim/opencode-compaction-guard

```jsonc
"plugin": ["opencode-compaction-guard@latest"]
```

It does two things: heals pending/running tool calls into error results before each request (covers the interrupted-tool case), and reverts the failed turn if the 400 still comes back (debounced, reversible with /unrevert).

To be straight about the limit here: the split you're describing lands after convertToModelMessages/normalizeMessages, which is past where the transform hook runs, so for that exact path it relies on the revert rather than preventing it. It's a stopgap until the real fix ships. Approaches are from #8497 and #1662.

If the error you got is the "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks" 400, that's a pretty common one after an interrupted tool call, and attachment/image turns seem to trigger it too. I made a small plugin that prevents it and recovers from it automatically:

https://github.com/viiqswim/opencode-compaction-guard

One line in opencode.json:

```jsonc
"plugin": ["opencode-compaction-guard@latest"]
```

It cleans up dangling pending/running tool calls before each request, and if the 400 still happens it reverts the failed turn so you don't have to throw away the session (you can /unrevert it). It's a stopgap until opencode fixes it upstream. The approaches are from #8497 and #1662.

If your error turns out to be something else (like a tool-argument validation failure), ignore me, this one's only for the tool_use/tool_result pairing error.

Duplicate of #33853 — same root cause: `ConfigVariable.substitute()` in `packages/opencode/src/config/variable.ts` silently resolves unset `{env:VAR}` to empty string. #33853 covers the MCP auth scenario; this issue covers the provider apiKey scenario. Closing in favor of the earlier report.

Confirmed on **Linux** and **Windows**, opencode **v1.17.11** — same root cause (`ConfigVariable.substitute()` in `packages/opencode/src/config/variable.ts` silently resolves unset `{env:VAR}` to empty string).

In addition to the MCP auth scenario described above, this also affects **provider `options.apiKey`** when used with `{env:VAR}`: the empty string falls through to the SDK, which sends no `Authorization` header (or `Bearer `\), resulting in `Failed to initialize provider "<id>". Check credentials and configuration.` The auth.json fallback at `provider.ts:1686` (`if (options["apiKey"] === undefined && provider.key)`) does not catch it because `"" === undefined` is `false`.

The code path is present on current `dev` as well.

Thanks for this fix — the MCP auth scenario is well covered and the "throw at config load" approach is the right call there (no fallback exists, so failing early is best).

However, there is a related scenario this PR does not cover, and the throw-first approach actually makes it worse: **provider `options.apiKey` with `{env:VAR}` + auth.json fallback**.

### The gap

A common pattern is to combine env-var-based config with credentials stored via `/connect` (auth.json) as a fallback:

```jsonc
{
  "provider": {
    "my-provider": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://api.example.com/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:MY_API_KEY}"
      },
      "models": { "my-model": { "name": "My Model" } }
    }
  }
}
```

Intent: use `MY_API_KEY` if set; otherwise fall back to the key in `auth.json`.

The auth.json fallback exists at `packages/opencode/src/provider/provider.ts:1686`:

```typescript
if (options["apiKey"] === undefined && provider.key) options["apiKey"] = provider.key
```

But this guard uses `=== undefined`, while `{env:VAR}` substitution resolves an unset var to `""` (empty string). `"" === undefined` is `false`, so the fallback never fires today — opencode sends `apiKey: ""` to the SDK, which sends no `Authorization` header, resulting in `Failed to initialize provider. Check credentials and configuration.` (reported in #33853 comments).

### Why the throw-first approach makes it worse

With this PR as-is, when `MY_API_KEY` is unset and the user relies on auth.json fallback, opencode now fails at **config load** with `missing environment variable: {env:MY_API_KEY}` — before `provider.ts:1686` ever runs. The user cannot use `{env:}` + auth.json fallback at all; they must choose one source exclusively.

### Suggested fix (complementary to this PR)

Change `provider.ts:1686` from strict equality to a falsy check:

```diff
- if (options["apiKey"] === undefined && provider.key) options["apiKey"] = provider.key
+ if (!options["apiKey"] && provider.key) options["apiKey"] = provider.key
```

This treats `undefined`, `""`, and `null` uniformly as "no key configured", letting the auth.json fallback take effect.

### Design question for this PR

Given the provider apiKey + auth.json fallback case above, would it make sense to:

- **(a)** Keep the throw in `variable.ts` (this PR as-is) AND fix `provider.ts:1686` in a follow-up — but then `{env:}` + auth.json fallback still breaks because the throw fires before fallback logic runs.
- **(b)** Switch `variable.ts` to warn-only (keep returning `""`) AND fix `provider.ts:1686` — this preserves the fallback path. But MCP auth loses the loud failure (back to the original problem).
- **(c)** Make the throw opt-in per field (e.g., a `missing` hint on the provider option schema) — more complex but lets MCP auth throw while provider apiKey falls back.

Option (a) alone does not unblock the provider scenario. Option (b) regresses the MCP scenario unless `provider.ts:1686` is fixed in the same release. Option (c) is the most correct but heaviest.

Would love to hear thoughts on whether `provider.ts:1686` should be fixed in this PR or a separate one, and whether the throw should be gated to non-apiKey fields only.

## UPDATE: Root cause fully identified

There are **two** `enrich()` functions in `main-D_cwiNV1.js`, at lines 74725 and 75932. Both merge server project metadata with local persisted cache (`childStore.projectMeta`).

- **Line 74725** `enrich()`: Used for the `projectsList` memo – **already** included `...childStore.projectMeta`.
- **Line 75932** `enrich()`: Used for `enriched` → `list2` memos (which feed the **auto-color assignment** at line 76023 and the **project avatar UI**). This one was **MISSING** `...childStore.projectMeta`.

### Startup race

1. Server sends project list via SSE → `sync2.data.project` populated (with lobster `icon.url`)
2. Second `enrich()` runs → `base2 = { ...metadata, ...project2 }` (NO local cache merge) → avatar shows lobster
3. Auto-color code (line 76035) checks `project2.icon?.url` → lobster URL is truthy → **skips** color assignment
4. Local persisted cache (`childStore.projectMeta` with `url: void 0`) loads async via `onPersistedInit` → first `enrich()` picks it up, but second `enrich()` ignores it entirely

### Fix applied (3 layers)

| Layer | File | Change |
|-------|------|--------|
| 1 | `dialog-edit-project-Cy5SF5th.js` | `project.meta()` patch includes `url: void 0`; `sync.set()` updater also clears `url`; `serverSDK().client.project.update()` called for local projects with `url: ""` |
| 2 | `main-D_cwiNV1.js` (line 74725) | First `enrich()` spreads `...childStore.projectMeta` over server metadata |
| 3 | `main-D_cwiNV1.js` (line 75932) | **NEW** – Second `enrich()` now also spreads `...childStore.projectMeta` |

### Relevant files

- `out/renderer/assets/dialog-edit-project-Cy5SF5th.js` — dialog save logic
- `out/renderer/assets/main-D_cwiNV1.js` — two `enrich()` functions, `projectMeta()`, `getProjectAvatarSource()`

I also want to add a more fundamental point: **undo/redo should never have been tied to git in the first place.**

OpenCode is positioned as a general-purpose AI coding tool. It shouldn't assume the user is "always inside a git repo." Real-world counter-examples are everywhere:

- Quickly fixing `/etc/hosts` or an nginx config
- Editing `~/.bashrc` or a dotfile, messing up, wanting to undo
- Experimenting in a fresh project that hasn't been `git init`'d yet

In all of these, I need undo — but I **definitely** don't need git. By coupling undo to git, OpenCode is effectively saying "no git repo, no undo." That's a strange limitation for a general-purpose tool.

**Claude Code's rewind has zero dependency on git.** It snapshots file content directly before each `Edit`/`Write` call, and restore is just writing those bytes back to disk. It doesn't care whether `.git` exists, whether repos are nested, or what state git is in. Undo is undo; git is version control — two different problems.

The multi-shadow-repo approach would fix nested repos, sure. But after the fix, the same limitation remains: step outside git and undo is gone. Better to decouple snapshot from git at the root.
